abstract: Anthropic launched the Anthropic Economic Index to measure AI's impact on labor markets by analyzing approximately one million anonymized conversations on Claude.ai. The analysis reveals that AI usage is concentrated in software development and technical writing, with 36% of occupations using AI for at least 25% of their tasks and only 4% using it for 75% or more. AI use skews toward augmentation (57%) rather than automation (43%), and is most prevalent in mid-to-high wage occupations like computer programmers and data scientists, while adoption remains low for the lowest- and highest-paid roles.
keyFindings: Software development and technical writing tasks account for the highest AI adoption, with the 'computer and mathematical' category representing 37.2% of Claude queries.
Approximately 36% of occupations use AI for at least 25% of their associated tasks, while only approximately 4% of occupations use AI across 75% or more of their tasks.

AI adoption shows a lean toward augmentation (57% of tasks) over automation (43%), with AI primarily collaborating with humans through validation, learning, and task iteration rather than replacing workers.
AI use concentrates in mid-to-high wage occupations like computer programmers and copywriters, with very low adoption rates in both the lowest-paying and highest-paying roles.
The 'computer and mathematical' occupational category dominated Claude usage at 37.2% of queries, compared to 0.1% for 'farming, fishing, and forestry' occupations.
methodology: Analysis of approximately one million anonymized conversations from Claude.ai Free and Pro plans. The study used Clio, an automated analysis tool that preserves user privacy, to match conversations to occupational tasks classified by the U.S. Department of Labor's Occupational Information Network (O*NET) database of approximately 20,000 specific work-related tasks. Conversations were organized by occupational task and task category, with salary data from O*NET used to analyze correlations between wage levels and AI adoption. A language model was used to filter data to include only conversations relevant to occupational tasks.
qualifiers: The authors acknowledge that Claude.ai data contains some non-work conversations and they cannot determine with certainty whether users were completing work tasks or personal projects. The study cannot establish how users applied AI responses (copy-pasting versus critical evaluation). Analysis is limited to Claude.ai Free and Pro users, excluding API, Team, and Enterprise users. Clio classification errors are possible given the large number of different tasks; Claude's inability to generate images directly may underrepresent creative uses. The authors note that coding may be overrepresented due to Claude's marketing as a state-of-the-art coding model. The dataset is not claimed to be representative of AI use in general. The authors explicitly state their research 'doesn't provide policy prescriptions' and that labor market impacts may change significantly as models become more capable.
